mainTopic: Intention and sin: a woman whose vow was secretly cancelled still needs כפרה, and the same act can be righteous or sinful depending on intention (לוט and his daughters)
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier discussion. The earlier משנה is about a husband who asked his wife, 'I am a נזיר, and what about you?', so he can cancel her vow while his own stays. A new משנה follows. A woman who broke her נזירות gets forty lashes. If her husband had secretly cancelled the vow, she gets no Torah lashes, though רבי יהודה gives her מכת מרדות. A ברייתא teaches from 'אישה הפרם וה׳ יסלח לה' that she still needs כפרה, and רבי עקיבא would cry over this with a קל וחומר: if meaning to sin needs forgiveness, a real sin needs it even more. The same lesson is drawn from the פסוק of אשם תלוי, with a single doubtful piece of fat and with איסי בן יהודה's two pieces, and the גמרא explains why all three cases are needed. Then רבי יוחנן explains 'כי ישרים דרכי ה׳': one act can be righteous or sinful depending on intention. After rejecting two examples, the גמרא settles on לוט and his daughters. It proves that לוט meant to sin and was not simply forced. The amud ends as רבא begins another teaching about לוט, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The earlier משנה is about a husband who asked his wife a question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the earlier משנה as a case where the husband said, 'I am a נזיר, and what about you?' So he can cancel her vow, and his own vow stays in force.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is talking about a husband who said to his wife, 'I am a נזיר, and what about you?' Because of that, he can cancel her vow, and his own vow still stands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an earlier discussion. It explains which exact case the earlier משנה is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband accepted נזירות fully on his own. He only asked his wife whether she wanted to join him. His vow does not depend on hers, so when he cancels her vow, his own stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: I am hereby a נזיר (the standard wording for taking on נזירות)
And what about you? (a question, not a condition)
Cancels a vow (a husband's power over his wife's vows)

steps.whatToRemember: The husband's vow is independent because he only asked his wife a question. So cancelling her vow does not touch his.

phrases.english: And the Mishnah is a case where he said to her:
phrases.notes: This is the earlier משנה where he says 'I am a נזיר, and you?' and she answers אמן. He can cancel her vow, but his stays.

phrases.english: "I am hereby a nazirite, and what about you?"
Because of this,
he can cancel hers, and his remains in force.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the earlier discussion by placing the earlier משנה in a specific case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The husband's words were a question, so his נזירות stands alone and is not tied to hers.

steps.title: A woman who broke her nazirite vow, and one whose vow was secretly cancelled
steps.stepSummary: A woman who broke her נזירות gets forty lashes. If her husband had already cancelled it without her knowing, she does not get the forty lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a woman vowed to be a נזירה and then drank wine or became impure from a dead body, she gets the forty lashes. If her husband cancelled her vow, she did not know about it, and then she drank wine or became impure from a dead body, she does not get the forty lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It compares two cases: a woman who truly broke her נזירות, and one who only thought she was breaking it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case the vow was real, so she broke a Torah prohibition and gets מלקות. In the second case the vow had already been cancelled, so she was not really a נזירה. Even though she meant to sin, there is no Torah lashing.

keyTerms.meaning: She vowed to be a נזירה
Making herself impure through contact with the dead

steps.confusionAlert: Her bad intention does not make her liable for the Torah lashes. Torah מלקות needs a real prohibition, and her vow was already gone.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
A woman who vowed to be a nazirite,
and she was drinking wine
and becoming impure from the dead —
she receives the forty lashes.
If her husband cancelled her vow,

phrases.aramaic: וְהִיא לֹא יָדְעָה שֶׁהֵפֵר לָהּ בַּעְלָהּ,
phrases.english: and she did not know that her husband had cancelled it,
and she was drinking wine and becoming impure from the dead —
she does not receive the forty lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה with a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Breaking a real vow of נזירות brings forty lashes. Breaking a vow that was secretly cancelled does not.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: she still gets rabbinic lashes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that even without the Torah's forty lashes, the woman whose vow was secretly cancelled gets מכת מרדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: even if she does not get the forty lashes, she should get lashes for rebelliousness.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds to the second case of the משנה. He gives a rabbinic punishment to the woman who meant to break her vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה agrees there is no Torah lashing, since there was no real vow. He still holds that her intent to sin deserves a punishment from the חכמים, called מכת מרדות.

keyTerms.meaning: Lashes for rebelliousness, a punishment set by the חכמים rather than the Torah

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
If she does not receive the forty lashes,
let her receive lashes for rebelliousness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a rabbinic punishment to the second case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meaning to sin, even without a real sin, deserves מכת מרדות.

steps.title: The verse teaches that she needs atonement
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the פסוק 'אישה הפרם וה׳ יסלח לה' as being about a woman whose vow was cancelled without her knowing. Such a woman still needs כפרה and סליחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: the פסוק 'Her husband cancelled them, and ה׳ will forgive her' is about a woman whose husband cancelled her vow while she did not know. It teaches that she needs atonement and forgiveness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives a Torah source for the משנה's second case. The source shows that this woman did something wrong, even without Torah lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is why the Torah says 'ה׳ will forgive her' if the vow was cancelled and nothing was broken. The answer is that the פסוק must be speaking of a woman who did not know about the cancellation and acted as if she were breaking her vow. Her intent to sin needs forgiveness.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The Sages taught:
"Her husband has cancelled them, and the Lord will forgive her" —
phrases.notes: במדבר 30:13

phrases.english: about a woman whose husband cancelled her vow
and she did not know, the verse is speaking,
that she needs atonement and forgiveness.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אִישָׁהּ הֲפֵרָם וַה׳ יִסְלַח לָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as the source for the משנה's case of a vow cancelled without the woman knowing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who broke a vow she did not know had been cancelled needs כפרה and סליחה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that wanting to sin is itself a spiritual wrong, even when no actual sin was done.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא cries over the verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא would cry when he reached this פסוק. He reasoned with a קל וחומר: if someone who only meant to sin needs כפרה, how much more does someone who actually sinned.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי עקיבא reached this פסוק, he would cry. He said: someone meant to pick up pork and picked up lamb instead, and he still needs atonement and forgiveness. Someone who meant to pick up pork and really did pick up pork needs it all the more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how רבי עקיבא reacted to the פסוק from the ברייתא. He draws a strong lesson about how serious sin is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The woman in the פסוק is like a person who meant to eat pork but actually ate kosher lamb. Nothing forbidden happened, yet the Torah says that person needs forgiveness. So a person who actually ate pork surely needs forgiveness even more. That is a קל וחומר, and it made רבי עקיבא cry.

keyTerms.meaning: How much more so (the ending of a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: Even meaning to sin, without actually sinning, needs כפרה. So a real sin is far more serious.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְשֶׁהָיָה מַגִּיעַ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אֵצֶל פָּסוּק זֶה,
phrases.english: And when Rabbi Akiva would reach this verse,
he would cry, saying:

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה מִי שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּון לַעֲלוֹת בְּיָדוֹ בְּשַׂר חֲזִיר,
phrases.english: If one who intended to pick up pork in his hand,
and lamb meat came up in his hand instead,
still needs atonement and forgiveness,
then one who intends to pick up pork in his hand
and pork really came up in his hand,
how much more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְשֶׁהָיָה מַגִּיעַ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אֵצֶל פָּסוּק זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a moral קל וחומר on the ברייתא's reading of the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If someone who only meant to sin needs כפרה, someone who actually sinned needs it even more.

steps.title: The same reasoning applied to the אשם תלוי verse
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא applies רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר to the פסוק about אשם תלוי. Someone who meant to eat permitted fat but ate a piece that may be forbidden fat still 'bears his sin'. So someone who meant to eat forbidden food and did eat it certainly needs כפרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Similarly you can say about the פסוק 'He did not know, yet he is guilty and shall bear his sin': A person meant to pick up lamb but picked up pork. For example, he ate a piece that might be permitted fat or might be forbidden fat. Even so, the פסוק says he 'shall bear his sin'. So a person who meant to pick up pork and did pick up pork certainly bears his sin.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a second פסוק that teaches the same lesson as the פסוק about the woman whose vow was cancelled. It builds the same kind of קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case here is a single piece of meat, and no one knows whether it is permitted fat (שומן) or forbidden fat (חלב). The person never meant to sin, and he may not even have sinned, yet the Torah says 'ונשא עונו'. If that person needs כפרה, then a person who knowingly eats forbidden food surely needs it even more.

keyTerms.meaning: And he shall bear his sin, meaning he needs כפרה
How much more so; the closing line of a קל וחומר

steps.confusionAlert: 'Lamb' and 'pork' here are just picture-words. Lamb stands for something permitted and pork for something forbidden. The real case is permitted fat versus forbidden fat.

phrases.english: Similarly, you can say:
'He did not know, yet he is guilty, and shall bear his sin,'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:17

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה מִי שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּון לַעֲלוֹת בְּיָדוֹ בְּשַׂר טָלֶה,
phrases.english: and if one who intended to pick up lamb meat in his hand,
and pork came up in his hand,
for example, a piece that may be permitted fat
or may be forbidden fat,
the verse says: 'and shall bear his sin.'

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּון לַעֲלוֹת בְּיָדוֹ בְּשַׂר חֲזִיר,
phrases.english: One who intended to pick up pork in his hand,
and pork came up in his hand,
how much more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the קל וחומר of רבי עקיבא to a second פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who may have eaten forbidden fat without meaning to still needs כפרה, so a deliberate sinner surely does.

steps.title: איסי בן יהודה gives the same reasoning with a two-piece case
steps.stepSummary: איסי בן יהודה reads the same פסוק with the same קל וחומר. His example is two pieces of meat, one forbidden fat and one permitted fat, where the person ate one of them without knowing which.
steps.simpleTranslation: איסי בן יהודה says about 'He did not know, yet he is guilty and shall bear his sin': A person meant to pick up lamb but picked up pork. For example, there were two pieces, one forbidden fat and one permitted fat. Even so, the פסוק says 'he shall bear his sin'. So a person who meant to pick up pork and did pick up pork certainly bears his sin.
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא, איסי בן יהודה, repeats the same קל וחומר, but he describes the case differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version the doubt comes from one piece of unknown status. In איסי's version there are two pieces, and one of them is surely forbidden, but the person does not know whether he ate that one. The conclusion is the same: even this person needs כפרה, so a deliberate sinner surely does.

phrases.english: איסי בן יהודה says:
'He did not know, yet he is guilty, and shall bear his sin,'

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה מִי שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּון לַעֲלוֹת בְּיָדוֹ בְּשַׂר טָלֶה,
phrases.english: and if one who intended to pick up lamb meat in his hand,
and pork came up in his hand,
for example, two pieces,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת שֶׁל חֵלֶב וְאַחַת שֶׁל שׁוּמָּן —
phrases.english: one of forbidden fat and one of permitted fat,
phrases.notes: He ate one of the two pieces and doesn't know which one it was.

phrases.english: 'and shall bear his sin.'
One who intends to pick up pork in his hand,
and pork came up in his hand,
how much more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the same קל וחומר with a different example case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even someone who ate one of two pieces, one of them forbidden, without knowing which, needs כפרה, so a deliberate sinner surely does.

steps.title: This is a reason to feel pain over sin
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the section: those who feel pain over their sins should feel it because of this teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: Over this matter, those who grieve should grieve.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up the emotional lesson of the whole section, much like רבי עקיבא's crying earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even an unintended or doubtful wrong needs כפרה, a person should realize how serious real sins are. This line turns the legal teaching into a call to feel regret.

keyTerms.meaning: They should grieve or feel pain

steps.whatToRemember: The woman whose vow was secretly cancelled, the doubtful piece of fat, and the two pieces of meat all teach one idea. Even someone who only meant to sin, or who may have sinned without knowing, needs כפרה. A real, deliberate sin needs it all the more.

phrases.english: Over this matter, those who grieve should grieve.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the closing lesson from the קל וחומר teachings
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Since even a doubtful or unintended sin needs כפרה, people should feel real pain over their actual sins.

steps.title: Why do we need all three cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא brought three different examples to teach the same קל וחומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do we need all these examples?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא gave three cases (the woman, the uncertain piece, and the two pieces) when they all seem to teach one idea. This question sets up the next steps, which will explain why each case is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three cases end the same way: someone who only meant to sin, or did not know, still needs כפרה. If one case could teach the lesson, the other two look extra. The גמרא wants to know what each one adds.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? This is the standard way the גמרא asks why something seems extra.

phrases.english: And why do I need all these?
phrases.notes: 'All these' means the three cases from before: the woman, the one uncertain piece, and the two pieces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the three ברייתות in steps 4, 6 and 7 and asks why all three are needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each of the three cases teaches that the others do not.

steps.title: The woman's case alone would not teach the uncertain piece
steps.stepSummary: If we only had the woman, we might say she needs כפרה because she meant to sin. The man with the uncertain piece meant to eat something permitted, so we might say he needs nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are all necessary. If the ברייתא had taught only the woman, I would say she needs כפרה and סליחה because from the start she meant to do something forbidden. But someone with a piece that may be forbidden fat or may be permitted fat meant to eat something permitted, so I would say he does not need כפרה and סליחה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer: every case is needed. First it shows that the woman's case cannot teach us about the uncertain piece.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The woman thought her vow was still in place and broke it on purpose, so her intention was bad. The man with the uncertain piece thought he was eating permitted fat, so his intention was good. That is why we need a separate case to teach that he too needs כפרה.

keyTerms.meaning: They are needed. This word opens a צריכותא, which explains why each case is necessary.

phrases.english: They are necessary,
for if it had taught only about the woman,
it is there that she needs atonement and forgiveness,
because from the start she intended to do something forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל חֲתִיכָה סָפֵק שֶׁל חֵלֶב סָפֵק שֶׁל שׁוּמָּן,
phrases.english: But a piece that may be forbidden fat or may be permitted fat,
where he intended something permitted,
does not need atonement and forgiveness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question in step 9 with the first part of the צריכותא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The woman's case alone would not cover someone who meant to eat something permitted. So the case of the uncertain piece is needed.

steps.title: The uncertain piece alone would not teach the woman's case
steps.stepSummary: If we only had the uncertain piece, we might say he needs כפרה because a prohibition may really be there. The woman, whose vow was truly cancelled, did nothing forbidden at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if only this case had been stated, I would say he needs כפרה because there may really be a prohibition. But a woman whose husband cancelled her vow did something permitted, so I would say she does not need כפרה and סליחה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes the other way. It shows that the case of the uncertain piece cannot teach us about the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the uncertain piece, there is a real chance he ate forbidden fat. With the woman, what she did was fully permitted because the vow was already cancelled. So we need her case to teach that even with no איסור at all, a bad intention needs סליחה.

keyTerms.meaning: Cancelled (a husband cancelling his wife's vow)

phrases.english: And if only this one had been stated,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the case of the single uncertain piece of fat.

phrases.english: [I would say he needs atonement] because there is a prohibition.
phrases.notes: The words in brackets aren't written, but they're understood. He may really have eaten forbidden fat.

phrases.english: But a woman whose husband cancelled her vow,
where it was permitted,
would not need atonement and forgiveness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second part of the צריכותא, the opposite direction from step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The uncertain piece alone would not cover a case where nothing forbidden happened at all. So the woman's case is needed.

steps.title: Why the case of two pieces is also needed
steps.stepSummary: Even with both cases, we might think כפרה and סליחה are enough only when the איסור was never clearly there. With two pieces, one was certainly forbidden, so איסי בן יהודה teaches that there is no difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if only these two cases had been stated, I would say that in these two cases כפרה and סליחה are enough, because the איסור was not clearly fixed. But with two pieces, one forbidden fat and one permitted fat, the איסור was clearly there, so I would say כפרה and סליחה are not enough. This teaches us that it makes no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by explaining why איסי בן יהודה's case of two pieces is also needed. It ends with 'קא משמע לן', meaning this case teaches us something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first two cases there was never a known forbidden item in front of the person. With two pieces, one was certainly forbidden, so we might think this is too serious for simple כפרה and סליחה. The ברייתא teaches that he is also covered by 'ונסלח לו'.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have said (a mistaken first thought)
The prohibition was fixed, meaning it was definitely there

steps.whatToRemember: Each of the three cases is needed. The woman: nothing forbidden happened, but she meant to sin. The uncertain piece: he meant well, but something forbidden may have happened. The two pieces: something forbidden was certainly there. All three need כפרה and סליחה, and all three can receive it.
steps.confusionAlert: 'לא סגי ליה בכפרה וסליחה' does not mean he needs less. It means we might have thought his case was so serious that כפרה and סליחה would not be enough for him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אִיתְּמַר הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא:
phrases.english: And if only these two had been stated, I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי הוּא דְּסַגִּי לְהוֹן בְּכַפָּרָה וּסְלִיחָה —
phrases.english: it is in these two that atonement and forgiveness are enough for them,
because the prohibition was not fixed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שְׁתֵּי חֲתִיכוֹת אַחַת שֶׁל חֵלֶב וְאַחַת שֶׁל שׁוּמָּן,
phrases.english: But two pieces, one of forbidden fat and one of permitted fat,
where the prohibition was fixed,
phrases.notes: One of the two pieces was definitely forbidden, so the איסור was really there in front of him.

phrases.english: atonement and forgiveness are not enough for him,
so it teaches us that there is no difference.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִיתְּמַר הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the צריכותא by explaining why the third case, איסי בן יהודה's two pieces, is needed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two-piece case teaches that even when an איסור was certainly present, כפרה and סליחה still apply.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Where the איסור was clearly there, כפרה and סליחה would not be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is no difference. He too receives כפרה and סליחה.

steps.title: Same act, different intention: the two people eating the פסח
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains the פסוק 'כי ישרים דרכי ה׳'. Two people eat their קרבן פסח, one for the מצוה and one to stuff himself. The first is a צדיק and the second a פושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: What does the פסוק mean, 'For the ways of ה׳ are straight; the righteous walk in them, and sinners stumble in them'? It is like two people who roasted their קרבן פסח. One ate it for the sake of the מצוה, and one ate it just to stuff himself. The one who ate it for the מצוה is 'the righteous walk in them'. The one who ate it to stuff himself is 'sinners stumble in them'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רבי יוחנן. It explains how the same 'way of ה׳' can make one person a צדיק and another a sinner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both people do the exact same action: they eat a properly roasted קרבן פסח. The only difference is their intention, and that decides whether they 'walk' or 'stumble'. This fits the theme just before it: what a person has in mind matters, not only what he physically does.

keyTerms.meaning: What is meant by what is written? This phrase introduces an explanation of a פסוק.
For the sake of the מצוה

steps.whyThisMatters: This opens a new section about intention, using cases where the same act can be good or bad depending on what the person has in mind.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
What is meant by what is written: 'For the ways of the Lord are straight,'
phrases.notes: הושע 14:10

phrases.aramaic: וְצַדִּקִים יֵלְכוּ בָם וּפֹשְׁעִים יִכָּשְׁלוּ בָם״ —
phrases.english: 'and the righteous walk in them, and sinners stumble in them'?

phrases.aramaic: מָשָׁל לִשְׁנֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם שֶׁצָּלוּ אֶת פִּסְחֵיהֶן,
phrases.english: It is like two people who roasted their Passover offerings,
one ate it for the sake of the מצוה,
and one ate it for the sake of overeating.
phrases.notes: Literally 'coarse eating'. He means stuffing himself, not eating for the מצוה.

phrases.english: This one, who ate it for the sake of the מצוה,
is 'and the righteous walk in them.'
And that one, who ate it for the sake of overeating,
is 'and sinners stumble in them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching on the theme of intention, after the צריכותא is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The same מצוה act can count as righteous or as stumbling, depending on the person's intention.

steps.title: ריש לקיש objects to calling the overeater wicked
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש challenges the idea that someone who eats his פסח just to fill up is a sinner. He still did the מצוה of פסח, even if not in the best way.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said to him: You call this person wicked?! Fine, he did not do the מצוה in the best way, but he still did the פסח!
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש attacks the example from step 13. He says the man who ate his פסח to stuff himself cannot be called a sinner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier teaching put the overeater into the 'sinners stumble' half of the פסוק. ריש לקיש points out that he still fulfilled the מצוה, just not in the ideal way. So the example does not fit the word 'sinners', and a better example is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A מצוה done in the best, ideal way

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the one who reported רבי יוחנן's teaching about the two people eating their פסח.

phrases.english: This one you call 'wicked'?!
Granted that he is not doing
the מצוה in the best way,
at least he is doing the Pesach!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: הַאי ״רָשָׁע״ קָרֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the example of the two people eating their פסח given in step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: Calling the person who eats his פסח to stuff himself a פושע
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He still fulfilled the מצוה of פסח, only not in the best way, so he cannot be labeled a sinner

steps.title: ריש לקיש's example: two men, each with a wife and a sister
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש offers a new example. Two men each have a wife and a sister in the house. One happens to be with his wife, the other with his sister. The first is a צדיק and the second is a sinner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: it is like two people. Each one has his wife and his sister with him. One happened to be with his wife, and the other happened to be with his sister. The one who was with his wife fits 'the righteous walk in them,' and the one who was with his sister fits 'but sinners stumble in them.'
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected the פסח example, ריש לקיש replaces it with a case where one person truly sins: a man who ends up with his sister.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the second man really did an עבירה, so the word 'sinners' fits. The two men started in the same situation, and the results came out very differently.

keyTerms.meaning: A parable or example that illustrates a point
'The righteous walk in them' (the first half of the פסוק)
'Sinners stumble in them' (the second half of the פסוק)

phrases.english: Rather: it is like two people,
this one has his wife and his sister with him,
and that one has his wife and his sister with him.
To this one, his wife came his way,
and to that one, his sister came his way.
This one, whose wife came his way:
'the righteous walk in them,'
and that one, whose sister came his way:
'but sinners stumble in them.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the פסח example rejected in step 14
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק describes two men in the same setting: one is with his wife (righteous) and one is with his sister (sinner)

steps.title: Objection: those are two different paths
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects ריש לקיש's example. The פסוק speaks of one path that people walk differently, but the two men did two different acts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it comparable? We are talking about one path. Here there are two paths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on ריש לקיש's example and says it does not match the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the same 'ways of ה׳' lead one person to walk and another to stumble, so it needs one identical act. Being with a wife and being with a sister are two separate acts. So this example misses the point of the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it comparable? (a sign that a comparison is being rejected)
One path, meaning one and the same act
Two paths, meaning two different acts

phrases.english: Is it comparable?
We are speaking about one path.
Here, there are two paths.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי? אֲנַן קָאָמְרִינַן חֲדָא דֶּרֶךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects ריש לקיש's example from step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's example of the two men with a wife and a sister
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק requires one identical act with two outcomes, while this example has two different acts

steps.title: The right example: לוט and his two daughters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives an example with one single act: לוט and his daughters. The daughters meant it as a מצוה and are righteous. לוט meant it as an עבירה and is a sinner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is like לוט and his two daughters with him. They intended it for the sake of a מצוה, so 'the righteous walk in them.' He intended it for the sake of sin, so 'sinners stumble in them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא replaces the rejected example with לוט and his daughters, where everyone took part in the very same act.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fixes both earlier problems. It is one act, so it is 'one path'. And לוט's side is a real sin, so 'sinners' fits. The only difference between them is their intention.

keyTerms.meaning: אברהם's nephew, whose daughters had children from him after סדום was destroyed
They intended, they had in mind
For the sake of a מצוה

steps.whatToRemember: The same act can be righteous for one person and sinful for another, depending on what each one intended.

phrases.english: Rather, it is like Lot
and his two daughters with him.
They, who intended it for the sake of a מצוה:
phrases.notes: See בראשית 19:31. They believed no man was left on earth and wanted the world to go on.

phrases.english: 'and the righteous walk in them,'
he, who intended it for the sake of sin:
'but sinners stumble in them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, מָשָׁל לְלוֹט וּשְׁתֵּי בְנוֹתָיו עִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a new example that answers both objections (steps 14 and 16)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק could be shown with the overeater or with the two men and their wives and sisters
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק fits לוט and his daughters: one act, with good intention on one side and sinful intention on the other

steps.title: Maybe לוט also meant well?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know לוט meant to sin. Maybe he too intended a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps he too intended it for the sake of a מצוה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the new example by asking how we know לוט's intention was bad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole לוט example depends on לוט meaning to sin. If he also meant well, there is no 'sinner' in the story, and the example falls apart.

phrases.english: But perhaps he too
intended it for the sake of a מצוה?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא הוּא נָמֵי לְשׁוּם מִצְוָה אִיכַּוֵּוין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind step 17
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that לוט intended an עבירה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Nothing has shown that his intention differed from his daughters', so he may also have meant a מצוה

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the verse about לוט speaks of sin
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that a whole פסוק about לוט is speaking about his drive toward sin. This shows his character, so we can assume he meant to sin here too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: This entire verse was said about sin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting רבי יוחנן. He reads a פסוק about לוט as describing a pull toward sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'וישא לוט את עיניו' looks like a simple description of לוט choosing land. רבי יוחנן says every part of it hints at sin. That proves לוט was a lustful person, so his intention with his daughters was not for a מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: Was said with sin in mind

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
This entire verse
phrases.notes: בראשית 13:10, 'וישא לוט את עיניו', when לוט chose the land near סדום.

phrases.english: was said about sin.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל הַפָּסוּק הַזֶּה עַל שֵׁם עֲבֵירָה נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof of character from a פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: לוט may have meant a מצוה like his daughters
steps.terutzMaskana: A פסוק shows לוט was drawn to sin, so his intention was for an עבירה

steps.title: Proving the verse's words point to sin
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן begins to go through the פסוק word by word. He shows that 'lifted up' and 'his eyes' are the same words used elsewhere in stories of desire.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And לוט lifted up': this is like 'and his master's wife lifted up her eyes.' 'His eyes': this is like 'for she is right in my eyes.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן proves his claim by matching words in the לוט פסוק to the same words in other פסוקים that are clearly about desire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Lifting up' is the word used for פוטיפר's wife trying to tempt יוסף. 'In his eyes' echoes שמשון wanting a פלשתי woman because she looked good to him. The shared wording shows the לוט פסוק is also about desire.

keyTerms.meaning: His master's wife (פוטיפר's wife, with יוסף)
She is right (pleasing) in my eyes (שמשון's words)

steps.confusionAlert: Each pair here is a word-match, not a story-retelling. The first quote is from the לוט פסוק, and the second quote is a different פסוק that uses the same word in a sinful setting.

phrases.english: 'And Lot lifted up':
like 'and his master's wife lifted up her eyes.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 39:7

phrases.english: 'His eyes':
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are the corrected wording. They're the next words of the פסוק about לוט.

phrases.english: like 'for she is right in my eyes.'
phrases.notes: שופטים 14:3

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבי יוחנן's claim in step 19 by going through the words of the פסוק
steps.raayaObject: That the פסוק 'וישא לוט את עיניו' is about sin
steps.raayaSupportSource: Matching words in בראשית 39:7 (פוטיפר's wife) and שופטים 14:3 (שמשון)

steps.title: The rest of the פסוק also points to desire
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן finishes the word-by-word reading. 'Saw', 'the plain of the Jordan' and 'well watered' each match a פסוק about desire or immorality.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And saw' matches 'And שכם בן חמור saw her.' 'The whole plain (כִּכַּר) of the Jordan' matches 'For a harlot, a man is brought down to a loaf (כִּכַּר) of bread.' 'For it was all well watered' matches 'I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drinks.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן keeps going through the פסוק about לוט. He links each phrase to another פסוק that speaks about desire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 20 he matched 'lifted up' and 'his eyes'. Now he matches the last three phrases, so the whole פסוק is read as being about desire. This supports his claim that לוט's character leaned toward sin, so he meant to sin with his daughters too.

keyTerms.meaning: Plain or round area, and also a loaf of bread. The double meaning is what links the two פסוקים.

phrases.english: 'And saw' — like 'And Shechem the son of Hamor saw her.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 34:2. This is the story of דינה.

phrases.english: 'The whole plain of the Jordan' —
phrases.notes: The word כִּכַּר means a plain here, but it can also mean a loaf. That's the hook for the next פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: ״כִּי בְעַד אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה עַד כִּכַּר לָחֶם״.
phrases.english: like 'For on account of a harlot, a man is brought to a loaf of bread.'
phrases.notes: משלי 6:26

phrases.english: 'For it was all well watered' —
like 'I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water,'
'my wool and my flax, my oil and my drinks.'
phrases.notes: הושע 2:7. The word 'drinks' (שִׁיקּוּיָי) comes from the same root as מַשְׁקֶה.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיַּרְא — וַיַּרְא אֹתָהּ שְׁכֶם בֶּן חֲמוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the word-by-word proof begun in step 20
steps.raayaObject: That the whole פסוק about לוט choosing the Jordan plain speaks of his drive toward sin
steps.raayaSupportSource: Word links to בראשית 34:2, משלי 6:26, and הושע 2:7

steps.title: But לוט was forced
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: לוט was drunk and asleep, so he was forced. How can he be called a sinner?
steps.simpleTranslation: But he was forced!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how we can blame לוט, since he did not know what was happening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if לוט had a bad character, someone who is forced (אָנוּס) is not held responsible. So the claim from step 17, that he meant it as a sin, seems impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: He was surely forced, meaning he acted without free choice

phrases.english: But he was forced!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim that לוט intended a sin
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim (steps 17 and 19) that לוט meant his act as a sin
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person who is asleep and drunk is forced, and a forced person is not considered a sinner

steps.title: The dot shows לוט knew afterward
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא in the name of רבי יוסי בר רב חוני explains the dot over the ו of 'וּבְקוּמָהּ'. לוט did not know when the older daughter lay down, but he did know when she got up.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in the name of רבי יוסי בר רב חוני: Why is there a dot over the ו of 'וּבְקוּמָהּ' (and when she arose) in the story of the older daughter? To teach that when she lay down he did not know, but when she arose he did know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from a dot written over a letter in the תורה. It shows that לוט became aware of what happened after the first night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says he 'did not know when she lay down or when she arose.' The dot weakens the word 'when she arose', so he did know at that point. This means he was not completely unaware the whole time.

keyTerms.meaning: Dotted. A dot written over a letter in the ספר תורה, which signals a special teaching.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר רַב חוֹנִי:
phrases.english: It was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rav Honi:
Why is there a dot over the vav
of 'and when she arose' of the older daughter,
phrases.notes: בראשית 19:33

phrases.english: to say that when she lay down he did not know,
but when she arose he knew.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר רַב חוֹנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge that לוט was forced
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual proof from a dot in the תורה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: לוט was unaware the entire time and was fully forced
steps.terutzMaskana: After the first night, לוט knew what had happened

steps.title: What could he do after it happened?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even if לוט knew afterward, what could he have done? What happened already happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what should he have done? What happened, happened!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. Finding out after the fact doesn't make לוט guilty for something he couldn't stop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 showed that לוט knew once the first act was over. But knowing afterward cannot change the past, so it still seems he did nothing wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: What happened, happened. The past can't be changed.

phrases.english: And what should he have done?
What happened, happened!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the usefulness of the answer in step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof that לוט knew when his older daughter arose
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Knowing afterward cannot make him guilty, since the act was already done and could not be undone

steps.title: He should not have drunk again the next night
steps.stepSummary: The difference is that once לוט knew, he should not have drunk wine on the following night. Drinking again showed he wanted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference is that on the next night he should not have drunk wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that לוט's fault was the second night. He knew what had happened, yet he got drunk again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first night can be excused. But since he knew, choosing to drink again put him in the same situation with the younger daughter. That choice shows he wanted the sin, which completes the proof for step 17.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical difference that comes out of this

steps.whatToRemember: לוט is called a sinner because he knew what happened after the first night (the dot on 'וּבְקוּמָהּ') and still chose to drink wine the next night.

phrases.english: The difference is

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְפַנְיָא אַחֲרִינָא לָא אִיבְּעִי לְמִישְׁתֵּי חַמְרָא.
phrases.english: that on the next night he should not have drunk wine.
phrases.notes: The next night was when the younger daughter came to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפְקָא מִינַּהּ, דִּלְפַנְיָא אַחֲרִינָא לָא אִיבְּעִי לְמִישְׁתֵּי חַמְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shifts the blame to a later choice that was in his control
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Knowing after the first night makes no difference, since the past can't be changed
steps.terutzMaskana: His knowledge mattered for the second night, when drinking again was his own free choice

steps.title: רבא begins a teaching on a פסוק about לוט
steps.stepSummary: רבא starts to explain the פסוק 'A brother offended is harder to win than a strong city.' His explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא taught: What is the meaning of what is written, 'A brother offended is harder to win than a strong city'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new teaching from רבא about לוט. This line is a setup: it quotes the פסוק, and the explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a fresh teaching, not part of the back-and-forth about whether לוט was forced. 'מאי דכתיב' tells us רבא is about to read this פסוק as a lesson about לוט.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written

phrases.english: Rava taught: What is the meaning of what is written,
'A brother offended is harder to win than a strong city,'
phrases.notes: משלי 18:19. The rest of the פסוק and רבא's explanation come on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new teaching about לוט after the previous discussion ended
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup only: רבא is about to explain משלי 18:19 as referring to לוט
